title: Rewriting the site after a pivot
metaTitle: Rewrite the site after a pivot
excerpt: After a pivot, the old pages are wrong in public. Rewrite the offer, redirect what you can, and take the previous product out of the navigation.
alt: A wide city avenue with yellow taxis, tall buildings, and people on the sidewalk, a street whose signs have to match the current direction.
caption: A street where the signs have to match the traffic. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the first thing to change on a site after a pivot?
faqs.answer: Change the sentence, the homepage title, and the navigation so they name the current product. Remove screenshots of the retired interface. Do the words before a visual rebrand, or the old offer will still be what people read.

faqs.question: How should old URLs be handled after a pivot?
faqs.answer: Redirect an old path to a page that honestly replaces it, ideally in one hop. If the old product ended, a short explanation and the new path is kinder than a silent jump to a generic homepage. Tell partners who link to you, because their articles will not update themselves.

faqs.question: What about customers still using the old product?
faqs.answer: Give them a clear note and a path, without letting that note become the whole homepage. Turn off public signup for a plan you no longer sell. Search the site for the old noun, including the footer and automated email, and replace it on purpose.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A website after a pivot is wrong until you change it on purpose. The old pages describe a product you no longer sell, to a person you may no longer serve. Redirect what still has a honest destination, rewrite the offer, and remove the previous product from the navigation. Leaving it up because the design is pretty, or because a URL once ranked, keeps the old company in public.

Do this before you write a launch essay about the new direction. The essay will sit next to a homepage that contradicts it, and the homepage will win, because it is what people open first.

## Wrong in public

Open the site in a private window and read only the navigation and the first screen. If they still name the old product, the pivot has not happened outside the building. Your investors may know. Your homepage does not.

List every place the old offer appears. The headline, the title in the browser tab, the meta description, the hero, the pricing names, the footer, the comparison pages, the illustrations with the old interface, the email signature, the deck you still send. The site is the one you can fix this week. The others should follow the same sentence, or you will rebuild the contradiction in the next call.

Say the new offer in one sentence before you touch the layout. Who it is for now, and what they get. If you cannot say it, you are not ready to redesign. You are ready to decide. A visual refresh on an undecided pivot produces a vague page that sounds like both companies. Visitors will pick the interpretation you did not want.

[Google's people-first content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is relevant here in a practical way. Pages should be worth recommending because they are accurate. A page that teaches the old product, or that wears a new date on an unchanged promise, is not accurate. Update the substance. Do not stamp a new season on last year's claim and call it a pivot.

## Rewrite the offer before the decoration

Change the words first, in a document, then in the interface. The first screen gets the new sentence. The second block gets the new proof, or it gets removed if the proof was for the old job. A screenshot of the retired interface has to go, even if it is the best image you have. A pretty picture of the wrong product is still an advertisement for the wrong product.

Rewrite the title of the homepage and of any page you will keep. [Google's title-link guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) says titles should describe the page, and that boilerplate fails people. A title that still says the old product name and the old category will keep attracting the old intent. That traffic will feel like a betrayal to the visitor and like a bounce to you. Write the title for the company you are now. If the name of the company stayed and the product changed, the title has to carry the new product. The logo alone will not.

Keep a short note of what changed if existing customers will arrive and panic. "We now do X. If you still need Y, here is the path." That note is respectful. A homepage that pretends Y never existed, aimed at customers who pay you for Y, is how support catches fire. The note can be a banner with an end date, or a page for existing customers. It should not be the entire homepage. New visitors need the new offer unobstructed.

Pricing and signup must match the new offer on the day you flip the homepage. If someone can still buy the old plan from a button on the new story, you have two companies again. Turn off the old plan, or move it to a page only existing customers can find, with plain language.

## Navigation is a list of current products

The navigation is not an archive. It is a list of what a person can do here now. Remove the old product's links. Remove the feature pages that describe retired capabilities. Remove the "solutions" that were really the old personas.

If you need the old story for a while, put it one step away, labeled as previous, and do not link it from the header. A header link is an endorsement. You are endorsing the company you are today.

Check the footer, the sitemap if you publish one, and the in-product links that dump people on marketing pages. The pivot often survives in a footer column nobody on the design team feels responsible for. Assign it. Read every link. If the destination describes the old job, fix the link or remove it.

Rename buttons that say the old verb. If you no longer "scan receipts" and you now "send the packet," a button that still says scan is the old product in miniature. These strings hide in components. Search the repo, or the CMS, for the old noun. Replace it on purpose, not with a blind find-and-replace that will also destroy a legal clause or a customer's name.

The same search belongs in the blog, if you have one. A post that recommends the old workflow will outlive the nav. You do not have to delete history. You do have to stop presenting it as current. A line at the top, with the date and the new path, is enough for a post that still has a point. A post that only made sense for the old product should redirect to the closest true page.

## Redirects that stay honest

A redirect is a promise that the new address answers the old question, or honestly replaces it. If the old URL was a product you killed, send people to the new offer only if you can say why on that page. A silent jump from a specific feature to a generic homepage feels like a mistake. A page that says "This product has ended. If you were here for it, here is what we do now and how to export" is a better destination, even if it is short.

Keep the redirect list in a sheet: old path, new path, reason. Implement the ones that have real inbound links, from mail, from docs, from partners. You do not need a ritual for every unused tag archive. You do need the paths printed on invoices, help articles, and the signatures of the sales team.

Do not chain redirects if you can help it. Old, to newer, to newest, loses people and makes the history unreadable. Point the old path at the current true page in one hop when you can.

Tell the people who send traffic. Partners, integration docs, and the friend who wrote about you. A redirect covers the click. It does not update their article. A short note with the new sentence and the new URL is part of the pivot. Otherwise their page keeps teaching the old you, and their readers arrive confused even when your redirect is perfect.

Test the important old URLs after the deploy, logged out. Include the ones in your own email templates. Those templates are a second site, and they are often still the old company.

## The rest of the surface

Social bios, the first line of the deck, the app store text, the invoice memo, the support macro. Pick the ones a customer sees and rewrite them to the same sentence as the homepage. A pivot that is only a homepage will be undone by the next automated email.

Images need a pass. Illustrations of the old workflow, icons that depict the old object, a hero video that narrates the retired pitch. Replace or remove them. Do not wait for a perfect new film. A still of the new product, or no image, is more honest than a film of the old one.

The portal or the docs you give customers should match. If Hanabi's own client portal is the model, it is a place for current files and updates, not a museum of every draft. Your customer-facing docs deserve the same rule. Archive the old manual where existing users can find it if they still run the old version. Do not let it be the first result for your product name.

If you have two products now, one old and one new, and both are truly for sale, the navigation should say so without blending them into a single vague headline. Two clear doors. One muddy door is how both audiences feel lost. Only blend them if there is a real shared offer. A pivot means the shared offer changed. Do not keep the blend out of nostalgia.

## A short sequence

Do it in this order so you never have a day when the new ad points at the old page, or the old page points at a new checkout that cannot sell.

1. Write the new sentence and the list of old terms to remove.
2. Draft the new first screen and the titles, before the visual polish.
3. Decide the redirects and the note for existing customers.
4. Ship the words, the nav, and the redirects together.
5. Then update the deck, the bios, and the automated mail.
6. Read the homepage aloud once a day for a week and fix the leftover old noun.

Resist a full visual rebrand in the same week unless the name itself changed. A new type system plus a new offer plus a new information architecture is three projects. The urgent one is the offer in public. Color can follow. A wrong sentence in a new color is still the wrong company.

If the new offer is not ready to be shown, the honest public site is smaller. A page that says who it is for and what they will be able to do, without pretending the product is on the shelf, is a different problem. That is the private product, and it is next: [a site for a product that is still private](/blog/a-site-for-a-product-that-is-still-private).
